title: Shade for Outdoor Learning
subtitle: Use observations and test results to improve a sunny school courtyard
summary: The class wants to learn outside, but the courtyard becomes hot. Listen to student observations, read a short science note, compare shade-test results, and recommend a careful first step.

briefing.scene: Your class wants to use the courtyard for reading and science. The sunny area can feel hot before lunch. The school has asked your planning team to study a small shade test and suggest what to try next.
briefing.goal: Use an observation and a test result to explain a practical recommendation, then apply your thinking to a new setting.

turns.speaker: Ms. Ortiz
turns.text: Our class meets outside near the west wall. On sunny mornings, the benches feel warm before lunch. The covered bench feels cooler, but only two students can sit there.

turns.speaker: Kai
turns.text: We tested three small model spaces for the same amount of time. The cloth-covered model stayed cooler than the open model. We should compare the readings before choosing a bigger test.

turns.speaker: Ms. Ortiz
turns.text: We have enough shade cloth for one bench. We cannot cover the whole courtyard yet. The team needs a safe plan we can try this week and check again.

report.title: Shade and surface temperature
text: Sunlight can warm a surface. A shade cover blocks some direct sunlight, so the covered surface may stay cooler than an uncovered one. The amount of shade can change during the day as the Sun appears to move across the sky. A reading from one time and one place does not tell us what will happen everywhere.

A class can compare two similar places by checking them at the same time. Students should use the same thermometer and wait the same amount of time before reading it. A shade cloth can help block sunlight, but it must be attached safely and checked for damage. The class should record more than one day of readings before deciding whether the change is useful.

phases.title: Choose a safe first test
phases.instructions: Use the observations, science note, and temperature table. Pick a first step that uses what the school has and leaves room to learn more.

decision.q: What should the courtyard team try first?

options.label: Attach the available shade cloth safely over one bench and compare readings there and at an uncovered place at the same time.
options.consequence: This uses the available cloth, follows the science note, and creates a fair comparison.

board.label: Test one covered bench against an uncovered place

options.label: Cover the whole courtyard immediately and assume every area will cool by the same amount.
options.consequence: This goes beyond the small test and assumes the result will be identical everywhere.

board.label: Cover the full courtyard without more readings

guided.model: I recommend testing the west bench first because the class wants to learn there and the school has enough shade cloth for one bench. Shade blocks some direct sunlight, so a covered surface may stay cooler. The cloth model measured 26 degrees Celsius, while the open model measured 31 degrees Celsius. These readings support trying a cover, but they came from small models. The team should attach the cloth safely and compare the bench with an uncovered place at the same time. It should collect readings on more than one day before making a bigger change.

frames: The cloth model measured ___, while the open model measured ___.
guided.model: Dear Principal, I recommend testing shade cloth over the west bench first. The cloth model measured 26°C, while the open model measured 31°C after ten minutes. Shade blocks some direct sunlight, so the covered surface may stay cooler. The class should attach the cloth safely and compare the bench with an uncovered place at the same time. We should record readings on several days before deciding whether to cover more of the courtyard. This small test gives us evidence without assuming every place will change in the same way.

guided.model: The test suggests that the shade panel may help keep a playground surface cooler. The shaded place measured 25°C, while the open surface measured 30°C after ten minutes. This comparison fits the idea that shade blocks some direct sunlight. However, the class measured surface temperature, not how comfortable students felt. The test also used only two places at one time. Students could repeat the readings on several days and ask classmates how the shaded area feels before recommending a larger change.
